title: Chapter 123 — The Musket
paragraphs: During the most violent shocks of the Typhoon, the man at the Pequod's jawbone tiller had several times been flung reeling to the deck by its spasmodic motions, even though preventer tackles had been attached to it — for they were slack — because some play in the tiller was necessary in heavy weather. In a severe gale like this, while the ship is but a tossed shuttlecock to the blast, it is by no means uncommon to see the compass needles at intervals go round and round. It was thus with the Pequod's; at almost every shock the helmsman had not failed to notice the whirling of the needles, though he cared little for such things at that time.

In a severe gale like this, while the ship is but a tossed shuttlecock to the blast, it is by no means uncommon to see the needles in the compasses, at intervals, go round and round. It was thus with the Pequod's; at almost every shock the helmsman had not failed to notice the whirling of the needles, though caring but little for the marvel.

Some hours after midnight, the Typhoon abated so much that through the strenuous efforts of Starbuck and Stubb — one engaged forward and the other aft — the shattered remnants of the jib and fore and main-topsails were cut adrift from the spars, and went whirling away to leeward like the feathers of an albatross.

The three corresponding new sails were now bent and reefed, and a storm-trysail was set further aft; so that the ship soon went through the water with some precision again; and the course — for the present, east-southeast — which Ahab was to steer, if practicable, was once more given to the helmsman. For during the violence of the gale he had only steered by instinct.

Instantly the yards were squared, to the lively song of "Ho! the fair wind! oh-ye-ho, cheerly men!" — the crew singing for joy that so promising an event should so soon have proven false the evil omens preceding it.

In compliance with the standing order of his commander — to report immediately, at any of the twenty-four hours, any decided change in the affairs of the deck — Starbuck had no sooner trimmed the yards to the breeze, however reluctantly and gloomily, than he mechanically went below to inform Captain Ahab of the circumstance.

Before knocking at his stateroom, he involuntarily paused before it a moment. The cabin lamp — taking long swings this way and that — was burning fitfully, and casting fitful shadows upon the old man's bolted door — a thin one, with fixed blinds inserted, in place of upper panels. The flickering light of the lamp revealed the loaded muskets in the rack. Starbuck was an honest, upright man; but out of Starbuck's heart, at that moment, strange things were bursting.

"He would have shot me once," he murmured, "yes, there's the very musket that he pointed at me — that one with the studded stock; let me touch it — lift it. Strange, that I, who have handled so many deadly lances, should shake so now. Loaded? I must see. Aye, loaded; and with powder in the pan — that's not good. Best spill it? Wait. I'll hold the musket boldly while I think. I come to report a fair wind to him. But how fair? Fair for death and doom — that is fair for Moby Dick. It's a fair wind that's only fair for that accursed fish. The very tube he pointed at me! — the very one — this one — I hold it here; he would have killed me with the very thing I handle now. Aye and he would fain kill all his crew. Does he not say he will not strike his spars to any gale? Has he not dashed his heavenly quadrant? And in these same perilous seas, gropes he not his way by mere dead reckoning of the error-abounding log? Shall this crazed old man be tamely suffered to drag a whole ship's company down to doom with him? Yes, it would make him the willful murderer of thirty men and more, if this ship come to any deadly harm. And come to deadly harm, my soul swears this ship will, if Ahab have his way. Great God, where are you? Shall I? Shall I? The wind has blown fair! — but is the fair wind my friend?"

"On this level, Ahab's hammock swings within; his head this way. A touch, and Starbuck may survive to hug his wife and child again. Oh Mary! Mary! — boy! boy! boy! But if I wake him not to death, old man, who can tell to what unsounded deeps Starbuck's body this day week may sink, with all the crew! Great God, where are you? Shall I? — The wind is fair. His sleeping hand is on the loaded musket."
"Stern all! Oh Moby Dick, I clutch your heart at last!"
Such were the sounds that now came hurtling from out the old man's tormented sleep, as if Starbuck's voice had caused the long dumb dream to speak.
The still-leveled musket shook like a drunkard's arm against the panel; Starbuck seemed wrestling with an angel; but turning from the door, he placed the death-tube in its rack, and left the place.
"He's too sound asleep, Mr. Stubb; go down, and wake him, and tell him. I must see to the deck here. You know what to say."
